title: Better than you’d expect.
text: so, after doing a ton of research i was able to conclude that this is for sure the best single wheel driven electric bike you can get for the price. i repeat, for the price! and in saying that, it’s actually a really great price. the box it came in was extremely well packed. in fact every single thing on it had its own bit of protection, which was awesome. the bike was 90% pre-assembled. there was very little to do other than attach the pedals, the handlebars, finish attachment of the fenders, etc. the typical stuff you’d usually expect. batteries came about 60% charged. of course i plugged it in and tried it out anyways to make sure it worked, and of course it did. before my first ride i charged up both batteries to 100% using the included chargers, which didn’t take as long as i expected. now the manufacturer states that it will get up to 28 mph and hold that speed on flat ground with an average load. i can confirm that this is true. the initial torque is actually quite good, and once you hit about 20 to 22 mph, obviously that torque wears down a bit. assuming you’re on a flat surface, and not carrying anything on top of you or behind you, it will actually get to 28 (eventually). the motor does make some interesting noise when it’s floating at full speed, but no big deal. on the plus side, you can actually get this up to 30 mph with some small changes to the p settings.  again, it won’t accelerate to that speed instantly. this particular motor and controller is set up to put out more torque than speed. as far as the range goes, i was able to get exactly 40 miles off of one full charge, and i suspect it could’ve gone at least another 10-12 if not more. i was doing a lot of stop & go which was super annoying lol, but not the bikes fault. the bike got a ton of looks everywhere i took it. everybody who sees it is very interested it. it’s such a unique and striking design. of course that’s one of the things that sold me on it, on top of the other positive points. i should also note that the “pedal assist” is more of a side effect than an actual function. the supplied gearing is very low. i never once took it out of seventh gear which is the top of the range for this model. seventh gear even at a high cadence will take you to about 10 mph max. after that, you’re on electric only. on the other hand, it does give you a way to pedal the bike in a slow crowd should you decide not to use the throttle, or to pedal home if you simply went too far. the brakes feel pretty good, and i love the fact that it comes with hydros as stock. not too many bikes at this price range have that (if any). as for comfort: for me i found that flipping the handlebar stem upside down made for a better riding position, but to each their own.  if in the future i’m looking for another rigid fat tire electric bike, i will certainly purchase another.

text: this is the 8th tent that i currently own.i have different tents for all occasions. from one person, uber lights, to 8 person, 4 season tents, i've pretty much got my bases covered.the intention behind ordering this one was to replace the super-budget, 6lb, 2-3 person dome tent that my daughter likes to take when she goes tent camping, (we usually hammock, but there are times when we have to use tents).she doesn't like the confined space of a one person tent like i use, so she's willing to pack a bit of extra weight for the increased living space.at a tad under 4 lbs total weight for this tent, she's shaved 2+ lbs off of her already heavy base weight...nice.the tent is 'mostly' free-standing. which means that it doesn't have to be staked out to be fully functional. this is important if you are setting up on solid rock or even loose sand. i say 'mostly', because you do need to stake out the sides to get the maximum square footage, but it's not critical if you don't.the rain fly is excellent and covers the entire tent, also providing a good sized vestibule to store gear or cook in during inclement weather.if you are 100% sure you're not going to encounter rain, you can leave the fly at home, saving an additional 1.5 lbs of weight and still have a bug-free, albeit less private sleeping area.all seams on the fly and bathtub floor are taped and showed no signs of leaking on the one night of rain she's spent in it so far.as with any tent in humid weather, expect some degree of condensation. because this is a two wall tent though, (separate body and rain fly), that is mitigated somewhat.overall i'm quite impressed with this tent.for the price i think it really can't be beat.you can spend 3-6× as much for a lighter, name brand option, but for the budget minded or a beginner who isn't exactly sure what they're going to need, this is an excellent option.very highly recommended.

title: A diamond in the rough
text: i was on the fence about buying this thing because it seemed really odd to me that i couldn't find a single yt review or reddit post or anything about this bike. it had more/less the same great looks as a super 73 for roughly half the price, but nobody had purchased it?  so i took the leap of faith and man...this thing is a blast.  first lemme get some of the negatives out of the way.  the manual is poor.  it's basically a single manual that they send with all their bikes, so it's more of an outline on how to assemble and use bikes in general, but doesn't give you many specifics for this particular model. the good news is that you can probably figure out how to assemble it by looking at pictures on the product page.  there was also a scuff on the front bottom left edge of the fork. it's nothing some touch-up paint can't fix, but there's that. the rest of the bike was in great shape and it was packaged well. delivery took about a week, which is acceptable.  i still don't know what the red thumb button on the left handlebar does. lol  i literally just got done with my first ride, so i have lots more to learn. the lcd is backlit and easy to see in broad daylight while wearing dark sunglasses.  the power is sufficient.  on flat/downhill sections, it was more than enough.  on uphill sections it was fine. it wasn't great, but it was fine. that's a common theme amongst e-bikes that may limit motor power so that they can remain trail legal. i know that's how it works where i live.  i maxed out at 27 mph on a flat section of trail, but there was a significant tailwind in my favor.  the seat isn't the most comfortable, but it's not bad either.  the lack of suspension is felt when off-roading, but once again..nothing major. the big tires provide more than enough comfort on trails and roads.  there's a lil switch on the side of the rear brake light to turn it off/on separately, which i thought was cool.  you can't use the throttle and shift the shifter at the same time, but virtually every e-bike is gonna be this way.  it's a heavy bike, as is the case with these moped/mini-bike styles, but you don't really ever feel it while riding because the motor picks up whatever you can't handle.  the pedal-assist allows you to dial in the level of workout that you want, and the throttle is there as a backup in case you need to cross traffic in a hurry. that throttle is especially important because the sensor that tells the pedal-assist when it kick in...it can be delayed a few seconds (once again, something i've heard most all e-bikes suffer from), so having the throttle there to get you up to speed immediately is a huge plus.  i can't stress enough how great this is.  if you're looking for an e-bike that's attractive, comfy, practical, but also lets you choose how much of a workout you want, this should be on your short list, especially if you can't bring yourself to spend 2x the price on some of the competitors. i do wish they had threaded inserts of accessories like a water bottle holder for my can of mug rootbeer, but that's on my long list of mods/customizations that i'll be tackling in the off-season.edit: the red button on the left grip turns the headlight on/off.

title: Good Quality, Good Value, Versatile Widths
text: i bought this to put on my forthcoming tracklocross bike, but it's on my commuter bike now, and will probably remain. well, it's lightweight, comfortable, durable, and it doesn't mark my pants. i was using brooks saddles, but they are (relatively) heavy and they mark up my sit area with oil or scuffs (the cambium ones have a denim cover that scuffs my pants). i also appreciate the understated logo graphics.i don't like to wear bike shorts except on long rides, and i don't care for any kind of gel or memory foam. the closed cell eva foam on this saddle is comfortable, and there is also some spring from the large-ish gap between the rails and the seat. i mean, on my 3 mile commute i don't notice the saddle at all, can't say about longer bumpier rides yet. i'm 6 ft, about 160 lbs, and don't usually have much weight on the saddle.so, i was unable to find many good reviews or descriptions on the pro line of saddles, but i will try to give my advice based on what i could piece together. the "offroad" line has two other models; the griffon and the volture. this one, the turnix is for moderately flexible riders, the griffon is for less flexible, or more upright riding, and the volture is for longer seated riding on an ebike. additionally, there are 3 widths, the wider being theoretically more comfortable for more upright posture. therefore, the 142 width will probably be most likely to fit most people if you don't have a known width preference. these have kind of a longer nose length more similar to a road saddle compared to the downhill mtb saddles. they have hollow stainless rails which i'm confident won't break on me. pro makes some road saddles with carbon rails if you want to take a chance and shave some weight. some reviews have complained that it's "slippery" but in my opinion if feels a bit sticky due to the rubberized details with my regular street clothes. i have to unweight to move around on the saddle.these are manufactured by shimano if you didn't know. my feeling is, while these are very well designed, shimano is in the process of designing the "perfect" balance of weight, shock absorption, comfort, style, and practicality or function and durability. i think they nailed it, but there seems to be some previous versions still available here on amazon. most likely you can find something comparable from other name-brands at a similar price point too, probably also in the process of ongoing design. this saddle has a somewhat old school vibe which i like.on amazon, you will see a lot of 25 dollar saddles that look great in the thumbnail, but if you can imagine producing a good quality bike saddle for $25, you can probably also imagine the difference in finish quality and durability. in my opinion, the pro line is a very good value for the price. (i bought a couple of the cheap seats on the 'bay; they are lightweight and you can sit on them, but they are noticeably crappy and less comfortable.one last thing is there is a mount on the bottom of the seat for pro-line of saddle accessories, but unfortunately they don't make anything useful to me at the moment; just a go-pro mount, and like a co2 mount, and a plastic ass-saver thingie. still, i might try to rig something with a bit of aluminum to mount there.tldr; i'm very happy with this purchase. i'm ordering a griffon model in 142 for comparison, and will use one for the commuter and one for the tracklocross (which will probably also be a commuter.)

title: I strongly recommend you seeing before buying it online
text: i’ve been aware of these products for about eight years, i’ve never seen one in person but the amount of reviews over that time on youtube from people i follow has been quite a few. the products looked to be good and i finally found myself buying one of their hip-bags.i’ve been carrying a shoulder bag for thirty years out of necessity and some have been with me for years at a time but none of them stay in place in any sense of the word as this maxpedition , if i elect to use the belt this thing is not going anywhere!the bag + shipping to the middle east + customs= $200 so needless to say my expectations were running high.i open the bag that it was shipped in and it was the wrong color. the paperwork correctly stated ‘khaki’ but the bag was military olive drab green. so that mistake made that bag unusable for me.but pressing on to the functionality of the bag. the gap between what i was expecting and what i was holding was fairly vast. now i mentioned it sits well- five stars for that.the first and foremost problem that should have been remedied is the waist strap. my waist is 42” and with some effort i can get it closed and it’s a nice feature if you’re concerned that someone is going to try and yank it away from you. but the part that is an epic fail is when you disconnect it and you no longer want to use it. this feature fails because at this point you either have to totally disconnect both ends of the belt—no easy task—or play with the thing for a good few minutes to shrink it down so that it isn’t showing and hanging about to look stupid and more importantly catch on things.another thing that i didn’t like about this bag were the compartments, they are in my opinion very specialized and if they don’t meet your needs exactly you’re carrying a lot of dead space. i’ll give you some examples of what i mean.to start with you have two pouches that are constructed well but they are limited as to what you can put in them. if i take my leatherman super tool 300 out of its carrying case it fits well but it is not ideal for care of that tool . some cans of pepper spray will fit others will not and i personally don’t carry it. a flash light would fit but i’m not so sure i would trust a $100-$150 flashlight to these pockets, a cheap one yes but not a good one.next we have the flap, i’ve got nothing to say about the velcro that’s for sheer silly business. the pocket would be fine for an id or some loose change a chap stick but nothing significant.the main compartment has this draw string “storm lid” and i can’t really see what the point of this thing is. it gives another good four inches of height but if you do so it doesn’t close with the flap! if you leave it tucked it you’ve got to wonder “what were they thinking?” when this storm shield is resting inside of the bag it is totally in the way of using the two side pockets that are on either side. i chose to place my flip wallet and my credentials here rather than on the outer pocket, what a pain it is to get the thing out.  so at the moment i have those items and two notebooks inside one is 1/8” thick the other is 1/4 “thick . for all practical purposes  my main compartment is full…for me i am going to need to take out this storm collar if it is ever to be used in any meaningful way.now we get to the space that they have a lot to answer for and that is the space they recommend for a concealed weapon. i’ve just told the few items i have in that central part of the pack --- it is nowhere near stuffed in the least and yet everything there encroaches on this space for ccw. the smallest gun that i have is a .380 and if i were to put it in there i’d have a dickens of a time getting it out. with a case that velcros inside that would be damn impossible without leaving the center compartment empty. to give you some idea on just how tight this thing is i wanted to put my eye glass case in there last night it measures 6”x2.5”x1” and it requires finagling. who wants to go through that just to get to their glasses?i’m not going to speak on some of the ridiculous things that maxpedition suggests to say nothing of some of the goofs on youtube when they talk about lashing things under the pack with the generous space provided. this isn’t a rucksack people, you’re going to put your bed roll underneath!another thing that needs to be modified is the handle. come on guys a nice rubberized grip or something of the sort didn’t cross your minds in the design process? you can doctor it up with a paracord handle if you’ve got the know-how but really it should be done for you at the factory.the side pocket is currently storing the belt from swinging about, if i put something in there then i have nowhere to store the belt, as i already mentioned there should have been considerable attention given to this idea before production.the most important fail on my trial with this bag is carrying it. as a professional tour guide this bag is on me off and on through a ten hour day and my neck and shoulder are so raw from the strap cutting into me it’s impossible to use as it is intended as a daily bag. besides the actual weight of the bag i have no more than ten ounces in it with credit cards, id a flash light and some pills. it’s ridiculous to think of adding even more lash ons to put more stuff, it simply can’t hold that weight and be comfortable.last but not least is the sound meter reading. if you’re a grunt, or in a tactical position where low noise is essential then you will want to know that the read out comes out to 80 decibels on the largest zipper which is equivalent to a busy street or alarm clock. the buckles and smaller zipper are in the mid 50’si would recommend seeing this bag before buying it making sure this is going to be a good fit for your needs. for a bag that’s made in taiwan i’ve got to wonder what production cost is and how much profit there is in each bag. i would expect a price tag to the consumer to range between $30-$40 beyond that it’s hard to justify the cost.

title: This survival kit needs some upgrades.
text: there is a saying “prepare for the worst, hope for the best.”  i would hope that i would never need to find out if i could survive in a wilderness environment but you never know.  i saw this survival kit and asked amazon to review it.i have experience in the wilderness, but i always had an idea of what i was facing.  i have backpacked in most of the western united states, alaska, and canada.  my longest trip was in the wind river range in wyoming.  it was harsh, beautiful, high terrain, and at night it could get cold.  i have helped rescue people who were not prepared.  it’s amazing what people think they can do without the proper equipment.different people will evaluate this kit differently based on their experience or lack thereof, their abilities, and their knowledge of the subject.  i have met people who would tell you this kit would be more than adequate, and it might be for them.  i am just writing this review based on my experience and what i think my abilities are.several years ago i took a wilderness survival class as part of an overall series on the out-of-doors.  i am not a survivalist, but i want to survive if something bad happens.  they taught me that you need to set your priorities when finding yourself lost in the wilderness.  they gave us “the rule of twos.”  first, within the first 2 minutes assess yourself for injuries.  if you have some take care of them immediately. second, within the first 2 hours find or make a shelter.  you need to stay dry and/or warm.  third, within the first 2 days, you need to find water.  fourth, within the first 2 weeks, you need to find food.  you can live a long time without food.  i thought using this rule would be a good way of judging a survival kit.first aid:  i would give this kit a c-.  it has a number of deficiencies.  i will list a few.  1.  it doesn’t have enough large bandages for large wounds.  2. the scissors are horrible.  they will not cut most things i tried them on, including the bandage material included. 3.  they give you about 100 q-tips.  in the many years i have backpacked, i have never had a need for a q-tip. you don’t want things you are unlikely to use.  4. they have plastic tweezers. they don’t work well at pulling out small things from your skin.  you need a good pair of metal tweezers.making a shelter and staying dry:  here i would give this kit a c.  it has a number of things that would be helpful in making a shelter.  however, the entrenching tool that is advertised is way too small to dig any kind of hole within a reasonable time limit.  the ax is very small.  it is sharp and will cut a 1 ½ inch branch but it takes a lot of time.  it has a number of saws.  the cable saw works best on dry wood.  i tried it on a living branch and got nowhere.  it provides a poncho and a lightweight emergency blanket, which reflects heat back to your body. they will help you stay dry and/or warm.  there is a sharp pocket knife that is large enough to be helpful.water:  here i would give this kit a d.  it has nothing to purify water.  there are no filters or pills to kill bacteria.  both are inexpensive and lightweight. the reason i gave it some points is that the poncho and emergency blanket can collect water or water moisture.  a problem is if you are collecting rainwater you need to decide which protective clothing you are going to use.food:  here i would give the kit a d+.  it has a knife and a small packet with things to catch fish.  it really isn’t very much.  there are only 2 hooks. i thought they should have put a quantity of dry bait in the package.  there is something that looks like a worm, but i'm guessing you are not going to catch a fish with it let alone survive. you could dig for worms but you're not going to survive on fish with only 2 hooks.what i have outlined are my major concerns. there are more but i have tried to keep this to several pages.  one of my overriding concerns is that there is no booklet telling you how to survive in the wilderness.  it doesn’t tell you how to build a simple shelter or the best ways to get water when there is not a stream around or how to trap small animals.  there should be a booklet that addresses the major problems you are going to face.  they give you a fire starter and two things that are probably very flammable. i have seen experts start of fire with a spark, but it requires knowledge and a lot of practice.  it is many times more difficult if things are wet. i think they should have included a lighter or at least some information on how to use the fire starter.  there won't be any youtube when you are trying to survive in the wilderness.finally, i can't emphasize enough the need to have a decent supply of duct tape in any survival kit.  it can be used for so many things.  it can be used for first aid, it can hold things together, it can repair tents, it can hold your shoes together, it can be used to repair tears in your clothing, you can use it as rope, and so many other things.

title: Save your money for a better quality tent that won't fail on first use.
text: final update~the replacement tent they sent was a lesser model, and it was actually dirty and used..with sand and grit all over the inside. still, i put it up in my back yard to see how it would do. it completed collapsed and filled with water, under modest wind and rain. completely unnacceptable. upon advising them of this situation and expressing my unhappiness at getting a lesser replacement tent that was used and dirty, they offered to refund my money and upgrade me to the colorado 8/9 tent. again, i was hopeful. however, upon first use, one of the poles is already splintered and the connecting shock cord broke.now, i've field tested three ntk tents~ cherokee 8/9, the oregon 8/9 and the colorado 8/9 tent models. they have all three been of poor quality and failed upon their first use, in my back yard, under moderate, reasonable weather conditions. i can't imagine the disaster if i got caught in a storm in of of these flimsy mesh bags. in light of this, i'm now down to one star, and i'd encourage anyone looking at ntk to look elsewhere.update~ i contacted ntk directly. they immediately responded via their chat message option on their website. they offered to replace  the tent, no charge to me. i understand qc sometimes misses a problem here  and there, i am accepting their offer of replacement. once i get the replacement and test it out, i'll revisit this review and update accordingly. i do very much appreciate how responsive their customer service has been, which also played into my decision to accept replacement rather than ask for a refund.i tested this tent in my backyard over 3 days of steady wind and rain. i didn't sleep in it, just wanted to see how it woud hold up in the elements. i was happy to find that it handled the wind fine. a small pool of water gathered in one of the corners due to a weak stitching job on the corner loop. but, i kept the tent and hoped for the best.i just got back from my first actual camp in the wilderness. i am sad and disappointed to report that the floor of the tent didn't hold up at all and now has mulitple holes, from dime-sized to smaller. i am an experienced camper. i've owned multiple tents of all styles and sizes over the years. i've never had a tent floor get holes like this. we keep our boots off and only use socks while walking in the tent. we utilized it exactly as it says it's designed for, as we have all our previous tents.we used a sturdy tarp as a footprint, and the ground was covered in fallen leaves, so it had a fairly gentle pitch spot. now that i've hung it up to air out, i'm noticing that all four corners have weak stitches and have already started to fray, after using this tent for two nights only.the floor looks plenty sturdy, like it's made out of rugged tarp material. it is actually quite flimsy. don't be fooled. it also is bowled and doesn't lay flat at all, whick makes it a constant snag and trip hazard.the poles held up in the wind, but with the low quality issues i'm already having, i wouldn't be surprised if they break, too.i do like the guyline system on the rain fly. the zippers worked great, without constant snagging. it is easy and fast to put up, but most folks will need another person to help. that's all the positives i have to say.i'm past the return date, so i'm stuck with it. i'll be putting tenacious tape on the holes and try to fortify the fraying corner stitches as best i can. most likely, i'll just continue to use my 6 person cabin tent and use this thing as an extra for friends to come along. i thought i was getting a good deal on a bargain tent that was made well enough to last 3-5 years of regular use. $200+ for a tent is only a good deal if the tent lasts more than one use before materials start failing. i'll start saving for the big agnes or the rei kingdom today.

title: Junk bearings
text: this is my first time venturing away from bones, and i regret it. these bearings have multiple areas that aren't good.1) they fit way too loosely over the axles, the wheels have too much lateral play.2) despite installing them flush into the wheels, the bearings themselves seem crooked and the wheels have a solid wobble.3) i get that bearings need to be broken in, but at least one wheel slows down to a stop real quick.4) one makes a raggedy sound just like old dry/dirty bearings do. as if something in there is asymmetrical maybe these are just qc issues and maybe they usually have a good product, but each wheel has an issue and all the bearings just have different sounds and things going on, none of them are consistent. more importantly, the first two points can easily lead to uneven or excess wear on the trucks and wheels, and that's especially problematic.update: just replaced these with bones reds. i examined them closer, the spacers were much wider than the gap in the wheel, so the bearings won't sit flush in the wheel. that gap between the wheel and bearing would've caused a lot of stress between the two bearing rings, increasing the risk of a dangerous bearing blow out. the bones have much thicker metal rings, they free spin much longer (the stingers slow quickly), and they have smaller ball bearings (less friction).the stingers also have really loose tolerances and a lot of play (which should be a really low abec rating). there's a lot of side-to side wiggle room between the two rings. you can kinda rattle them. there's machine marks on the ring side faces. the rings also have beveled edges (less surface contacting axle and wheel), and by spinning them, you can see the beveling is ever so slightly uneven on a few (the width of the outside ring surface changes). spinning them and looking from the side, there's an uneven wobble you can see in some of the racers, and at least one seemed to have uneven thickness to the outer ring. another one when rolled across glass had a jerky/rough spot in it's rotation. none of that indicates "precision", but it definitely indicates a possible injury if you're bombing a hill on these.

title: Great concept, poor performance
text: the concept is extremely well thought out but the performance is just so poor rendering this gadget useless.the idea is, as you can see, this zero sight system makes a spot on the target.  then after a shot is made, align your rifle back to the exact original spot by using the laser marking you made earlier.  then adjust your firing scope to meet the actual point of impact (calibrating for trajectory rise of course).. and voila.sounds incredibly simple and brilliant, right? and it is!  but here's the problem.1.  the zero sight is so badly calibrated itself the two lasers do no travel sufficiently parallel so by 100 yrds the spread of two lasers is soooo huge it's more than 6 feet wide.  yes sure if you use the broad side of the barn as your target, then yes, this works.  otherwise there's no way you can simultaneously put two laser markings on a typical 18 inch piece of paper or even 24 inches.  most of your sighting targets are 18 or 24 inches wide with 6 inch circles.  try put two laser dots 6 feet wide on that.2.  light dispersion.  at 10 feet the laser dot is micro millimeter and that is awesome.  at 100 yrds... you've got a 2 inch dot.  good luck pin point exactly where your laser making was even if you could put those on a 6 feet wide sheet of paper.now you wonder ehh why do you need two parallel dots and why can't 1 dot work?  actually yes in theory you can because it's the same concept on how this laser assisted alignment works.  but... but.. one dot you have to be careful to align the rifle back exactly and not slightly rotated.  two dots will be clearly visible that your rifle has rotated slightly.  in other words you can reposition the laser dot exactly back on where it was but that does not guarantee your rifle is where it was.  try this with any single-dot laser pointer.  you can rotate it and the dot will stay put.  now bundle two laser pointers together, and you'll see you have to orient precisely otherwise the two dots won't align.  try and you'll see.bottom line is.. yes this product's concept is brilliant but it just performed so poorly at distance.ok so why not try scope in the rifle at 25 yrds?  for that matter why not just scope in at 7 yrds?  that just defeats the entire purose isn't it?  you need 100 yrds of precision to know where you'll hit at 500 yrds.  this device just doesn't perform at 100 yds (but can at 7 yrds). if you are only scoping in your rifle for 100 yrds effectiveness then yes..... but if 100 yrds accuracy is all you need, you don't need laser assisted sight system.  so, complete paradox here!hope this helps.

title: Read this if you’re trying to decide between a Gear Fit 2 and Fitbit Charge 2!
text: after a ton of research about fitbit products, i purchased the fitbit charge 2 as an upgrade to my fitbit one. i had to return/exchange the charge 2 as the step count was wildly inaccurate. fitbit advised that this was a defect and provided a new device promptly. however, the new device had the exact same issue.  both charge 2’s have been returned.i then broadened my research beyond fitbit products and was stunned to learn at how much more i could get for my money if i opened my mind beyond the popular fitbit product line. i ended up purchasing a samsung gear fit 2 and am very happy i did.i’ve used the charge 2 and gear fit 2 each for at least a month, and here’s my take on how they compare -*accuracy:this is the main deciding factor for me. the charge 2 was wildly inaccurate (keep in mind, i received 2 devices from fitbit as noted above – both with the same issue). it consistently missed over 1,500 steps a day and counted steps while i slept somehow.  my fitbit one didn’t have this issue. fitbit customer support suggested i place the charge 2 in my pocket for improved accuracy, which completely negated the purpose of upgrading from the one to the charge 2.the gear fit 2 is pretty spot on. i say ‘pretty’ because the only time it’s slightly off is when i walk in place, and that’s ok with me because i’m cheating anyway…  it also accurately counts repetitions when using the different exercise features (lunges, crunches, squats), which is really cool and helpful.*features/functionality:the gear fit 2 is the clear winner here.  the biggest reason is that if you’re looking to keep track of how you’re doing with your fitness goals, even if you’re just casually trying to improve your fitness level, it really makes it easy by improving awareness. for example, when viewing any item such as floors or steps, not only do you see today’s activity, but you also see how you did for the rest of the week at a glance. tapping on those screens displays the detail by day. you can get more detail on the exercise done (map, etc) if you want to from these screens as well. there's really not much of a need to use the app with the gear fit 2.the charge 2 will display this detail within the app only, as far as i know.i tried the guided breathing feature on the charge 2 a few times and didn’t really find any value in it. to each their own.the gear fit 2 has built in gps (no phone required!), so once you’re done with your run/walk/hike, you can view your route, distance, average mph and much more, right on your wrist.myfitnesspal works really well with the gear fit 2 so you can quick add foods directly from your wrist and log water intake with a couple of taps.with the gear fit 2, i can play music from my phone or store music directly on the device. i can view/dismiss alarms directly from the screen. i love the ability to set a button to quick launch a feature. i use it to quick launch an exercise, so all i have to do is press the button, and i’m off! on the charge 2, you’d have to tap thru the screens, then press/hold to launch the exercise - this was kind of a pita for me and i usually forgot to do it before i set off on my adventure.one thing that i really love, which may not be a big deal to many other folks, is the ability to quickly set the gear fit 2 to ‘do not disturb’ mode. this means that the all alerts are muted and device won’t wake when you move your wrist. it’s great to use when sleeping so you don’t light up the room at night!*comfort:the gear fit 2 blows the charge 2 away here. you can tell by the photo that the charge 2 doesn’t sit flush to the wrist area, largely due to the lumpy bottom and straight face. this made me abundantly aware that i had something on my wrist every second of every day that i wore it. it was downright painful to wear while sleeping if i put any pressure on that wrist (if i slept on that side). when i took the charge 2 off to charge it or shower, i had a visible indentation mark on my wrist from it (and i wasn’t wearing it too tight).the gear fit 2 has a curved display with a flush bottom that i forgot i was wearing once the novelty of playing with it wore off. it’s comfortable to wear while sleeping and while active.*customization: it’s kind of a split here, but i’d have to say that overall, the gear fit 2 wins.the charge 2 has the advantage over the gear fit 2 in the band category since there are so many different bands to choose from. i’m really not sure why there aren’t more available for the gear fit 2, but i will say that i’m happy with the options that i’ve found.  there’s a great magnetic milanese one out there that i love. and, for anyone else who’s lost some thumbnails – it’s easier to remove the original gear fit 2 band if you bend it backwards a little bit:)the gear fit 2 wins over the charge 2 with respect to the customization features available directly within the device. for example, with the gear fit 2, the biggest difference is that you have a color screen. so, you have a whole world of options open to you for different clock screens. i can easily change mine each day to match my outfit. then, there are all the different apps you can download and use right on your wrist (such as myfitnesspal and workout trainer).*battery life:it’s a draw.  some complain that the gear fit 2 has too short of a battery life,
